# AUDIT — PR #37 `fix(sem): disambiguate same-name overloads in semantic diff`

Repo `entireio/entire-graph` · head `b4e0d5d` · base `main` (`fafe928`). Scope: `internal/sem/analyze.go` (+66-8), `internal/sem/analyze_test.go` (+247).

## Bug being fixed (confirmed understanding)
Old `compareEntities` keyed entities by `key() = Kind:Name` into `beforeByKey`/`afterByKey` maps. Same-name/same-Kind overloads (reachable in C#/Java; TS collapses them) collided under last-write-wins → only the last one in file order survived, so an edit to the first overload vanished (issue #35). New `keyedEntityMaps` replaces that with two-phase keying: Phase 1 pairs exact `Kind:Name:Signature` by occurrence index (prefix `=`); Phase 2 assigns leftover same-`Kind:Name` entities positional ordinals (prefix `~`).

## Core correctness (Pass A) — CONFIRMED SOUND
- **No entity is ever lost.** Every entity receives a unique key on its side: phase-1 keys `=sk#occurrence` are unique per `sk` per side; phase-2 keys `~KindName#leftoverSeen` are unique per `Kind:Name` per side; `=`/`~` prefixes prevent cross-phase collision. Map size == entity count on each side. This is exactly the property whose absence caused #35 — verified by construction (`analyze.go:427-441`).
- **Matching key is name+signature (phase 1), falling back to name+position (phase 2)** — not arity, not raw position. Phase-1 exact match means *unchanged* overloads pair regardless of file position; only genuinely-differing ones reach positional pairing. This is what makes reorder/mid-insert/mid-remove inert for untouched overloads.
- **Phase-1 condition `occurrence < otherSigs[sk]` is correct and symmetric.** Each side sends its first `min(beforeCount, afterCount)` occurrences of a given `sk` to phase 1 with matching indices `#0..#min-1`; the rest fall to phase 2. No off-by-one.
- **Asymmetric counts handled correctly.** Added-overload → sole phase-2 leftover on after side → one `added` (verified logic + `TestCompareEntitiesAddedOverloadReportedAsAdded`). Removed-overload → symmetric (`...RemovedOverloadReported`, `...RemoveFirstOverloadNoCascade`). Confirmed by hand-tracing #35 repro and the 3-overload remove-first case.
- **Phase-2 pairs always have differing signatures** (equal signatures would have been phase-1 matched), so phase-2 can only yield `signature_changed`/`removed`/`added`, never a mis-emitted `body_changed`. Body-change confusion is confined to phase 1 (same-signature) only.
- **Non-overload common path preserved.** Single unchanged entity → phase-1 exact match (no event); single edited entity → sole phase-2 leftover both sides → `signature_changed`; body-only change → phase-1 match → `body_changed`. Identical to prior behavior (`...SingleEntityUnchangedBehavior`).
- **Rename/move reconcilers untouched and unaffected.** `bestRename`/`reconcileMoves` treat keys as opaque; in-place overload edits are resolved in phase 2 *before* reaching `bestRename`, which is precisely why the PR (correctly) rejects a naive pure-signature key that would regress #35 to remove+add.
- **No new O(n²).** `keyedEntityMaps` is O(n) (three linear map passes/side). `bestRename` O(deleted×added) and `reconcileMoves` O(removed×added) are pre-existing, unchanged.
- `fmt` already imported; no dead code; `key()` still used by phase 2; no stale callers of removed inline keying (grep-verified).

## Adversarial (Pass B)
- (a) 3+ overloads, one signature edited → exactly one `signature_changed`, no cascade. **CONFIRMED** (trace + `...RemoveFirstOverloadNoCascade`, `...DisambiguatesSameNameOverloads`).
- (b) identical `Kind:Name:Signature` duplicates, edit one body → one `body_changed` via occurrence-index pairing. **CONFIRMED** (`...TrueDuplicatesEditOne`).

A `Signature` containing `#` (or `Name` containing `:`) could in principle produce a key-string ambiguity. `:` is pre-existing style; `#` is newly introduced as the ordinal delimiter. # AUDIT — PR #39 `fix(sem): surface parse failures in diff instead of phantom removals` (entireio/entire-graph)

## What the fix does (verified against source)
`AnalyzeGitRange` now parses both sides with `ParseWithStatus` and gates the per-file delta on `ParseStatus.ParseError`:
- **Total failure** (`ParseError && len(entities)==0`) on either side → append a machine-readable `parseFailureWarning(...,suppressed=true)` and `continue` (skip the whole file delta — no phantom removed/added).
- **Partial recovery** (`ParseError && len(entities)>0`) → append `parseFailureWarning(...,suppressed=false)` but **keep** the diff.
- **Clean / legitimately-emptied** (`ParseError==false`) → untouched; real `removed` changes stand.
`result.Warnings = reconcileMoves(...)` was correctly changed from assignment to `append`, so parse warnings survive alongside move warnings. `text.go` adds `writeTextWarnings` rendering (previously text ignored `Warnings`).

## Build / test (read-only)
- `go build` OK, `go vet` OK.
- `go test ./internal/sem/` → **658 pass**; targeted `Parse|Diff|Analyze|Text|Warn` → 118 pass.
- **Revert-verification** (via `go test -overlay`, repo untouched): with analyze.go+text.go reverted to `main`, the new behavioral tests **FAIL** — `AddedFileUnparseable`, `DeletedFileUnparseable`, `BothSidesUnparseable`, `SoftErrorWithEntitiesKeptWithWarning`, `PartialRecoveryKeepsDiffWithWarning`, `ParseFailurePreservedWithReconcileWarning`, `SurfacesParseFailures`, `WriteTextRendersWarnings*`. ## Pass A (careful) — does it distinguish parse-failure from legitimate removal?
**YES, correctly.** Suppression fires only on `ParseError && zero entities`. A cleanly-emptied valid file has `ParseError==false` (tree-sitter recovers a root with no error nodes; YAML `root.HasError()`; Groovy `braceErrors>0`) → never suppressed → its real `removed` changes are reported. This is the crux, and it holds. Explicitly covered by `SurfacesParseFailures/"genuinely emptied file still reports real removals with no warning"` (base=alpha+beta valid → head=`// all symbols removed` → asserts real removed alpha+beta AND no warning).

Warning propagation is complete: every suppression path appends a warning **before** `continue` — there is **no silent drop**. Side-selection logic (`afterStatus,path` default; flip to `beforeStatus,oldPath` only when the after side isn't the failing one) is correct in both the suppressed and partial branches. `if/continue` then a plain `if` (not else-if) — but the `continue` guarantees no double-warning per file.

## Pass A — the two fixed masks (CONFIRMED CORRECT)

**TS static-accessor** `parser.go:395/466` — `(\bstatic\s+accesso)r(\s*\()` → `"${1}R${2}"`. Only the literal `r`(1B)→`R`(1B); both whitespace runs are captured groups reproduced verbatim. Byte-invariant for *any* input. Match set identical to the old pattern (same `\b…static\s+accessor\s*\(`), so no over/under-match regression; negative form `static accessor x=1` still doesn't match. Neutralization intent (rename `accessor`→`accessoR` so it isn't the contextual keyword) preserved.

**Java module-import** `parser.go:622/636` — `^(\s*import\s+)module(\s+)` → `"${1}      ${2}"` (exactly 6 spaces). `module`(6B)→6 spaces; trailing whitespace now captured as `${2}` and re-emitted verbatim. Byte-invariant for any whitespace count. Single-space output is byte-identical to the pre-fix output, so no neutralization regression.

Empirically verified byte-length invariance (standalone regex replica) across multi-space, tabs, mixed ws, embedded CRLF, and multibyte Unicode around the match: TS 16→16, 17→17, 19→19, 39→39 (`中文`/`éé`), 18→18 (CRLF); Java 24→24, 26→26, 36→36 (`中文`), tabs preserved. The claim rests entirely on sub-premise (b): "Go's os/exec passes duplicates through to execve unchanged (it does not dedup)." **That premise is false.**

Decisive proof — I ran a child process with `cmd.Env = append([...,"LC_ALL=fr_FR.UTF-8",...], "LC_ALL=C", "LANG=C")` (exactly `newCmd`'s shape). Parent slice contained BOTH `LC_ALL` entries; the child's actual environ contained **exactly one**:

CHILD_ENVIRON_LC_ALL_ENTRIES=1 [LC_ALL=C]
CHILD_GETENV_LC_ALL="C"
```
Source confirms why: `Cmd.environ()` (exec.go:1223) calls `dedupEnv` → `dedupEnvCase`, whose comment reads *"preserve the last occurrence of each key."* The dedup is **unconditional** — only the case-insensitivity flag is `GOOS=="windows"`-gated — and `exec.go` carries no build tag, so it compiles and runs identically on Linux. git therefore never sees a duplicate `LC_ALL`; it receives a single `LC_ALL=C`.

- (a) glibc-getenv-returns-first is roughly correct (glibc, and darwin, scan environ front-to-back), **but moot** — there is no duplicate for getenv to disambiguate.
- (c) Reachability: none. No parent `LC_ALL` value, in any container or prod env, can defeat the pin, because Go collapses the append to last-wins before `execve`.

Honest severity: **NONE**. The pin is correct on every platform.

`TestNewCmdPinsSubprocessLocaleToC` does check the raw `cmd.Env` slice's last `LC_ALL`/`LANG` (the loop overwrites, so it captures the last occurrence) rather than running git. But because Go's dedup keeps the **last** slice entry, "last value in `cmd.Env`" is exactly what the child git process receives — so the assertion is a **valid proxy** for the effective pin, not false confidence about a real failure mode (there is none, per #1). Fair residual: it's a weak test (never launches git under a translated locale), so it wouldn't catch a future regression that changed *how* env is passed. Worth a one-line note, not a blocker.

What you're looking at is the **loops→graphs** shift. A loop = one agent cycling (plan→act→verify). A graph = many agents as an **org**: compute nodes + shared state + feedback + rules that let the org **rewrite itself at runtime**. The image is a self-reorganizing content org. You already have every primitive to build one here — you've watched it run this session (the 5-agent audit fan-out + verify pass, the comprehension workflow = readers→synthesis, were graphs).

## The image → what you actually have

| Image node | Primitive here |
|---|---|
| **SHUBHAM** (goals·taste·approval) | You — the authority node. `AskUserQuestion` / plan-gates are the edges into it |
| **MONICA** (control plane·org designer) | The orchestrator + the **Workflow** script's control loop — the thing that decides *who runs* |
| **DWIGHT / ROSS** (research / build) | `agent()` work nodes with roles |
| **SHARED STATE** (signals·thesis·feedback·memory/**gbrain**) | Files on disk + the **entire brain** (facts + semantic). Literally "shared files are state"; gbrain ≈ the brain |
| **KELLY / RACHEL / PAM** → X/LinkedIn/newsletter | Per-channel transform agents (leaves) |
| **AUDIENCE SIGNALS** (metrics·replies·clicks) | A *measure* node that writes metrics **back** into shared state |
| **RUNTIME REORG EVENTS** row | `if` branches in the loop that change the graph (see below) |

## The 5 pieces that make ANY self-prompting graph
1. **Compute = agents.** Stateless workers, spawned per task.
2. **State = shared files + brain.** Durable, every node reads/writes. NOT an agent.
3. **Edges = control flow.** `pipeline` (stream), `parallel` (barrier), `if` (route).
4. **Feedback = the loop-closer.** Output+metrics of round N become the *input/prompt* of round N+1. This is the whole trick — "the system prompts itself" = the next prompt is composed **from state**, not typed by you.
5. **Reorg = conditionals on metrics.** The image's bottom row *is* the code: `2× fix → promote model`, `failure cluster → add review board`, `budget > progress → collapse fan-out`, `small task → run solo`. The graph shape is an **output**, not a fixed input.

## Skeleton (runnable as a Workflow here)
```js
let state = load(goal)                        // SHARED STATE / brain
while (!done(state) && budget.remaining() > floor) {
  const plan = await agent(controlPrompt(state), {schema: PLAN})   // MONICA: decides nodes+prompts
  const work = await parallel(plan.nodes.map(n => () => agent(n.prompt, {schema: OUT})))  // DWIGHT/ROSS/KELLY…
  const metrics = await agent(measurePrompt(work), {schema: METRICS})  // AUDIENCE SIGNALS
  state = merge(state, work, metrics)         // write back → next round's input
  if (metrics.failClusters) plan.addCritic()  // ← runtime reorg
  if (budget.spent() > progress) plan.collapseFanout()
}
```
"Self-prompts itself" = `controlPrompt(state)` generates round N+1's prompts from round N's results. You only set `goal` + approve.

## How many agents
No fixed number — it's a function, not a constant:
- **Core shape:** `1 control-plane + N work nodes (one per independent sub-task/channel) + 1 critic/verify`. The image ≈ 1 + 2 + 3 + 1 ≈ **7 real agents** (SHUBHAM = you, SHARED STATE/leaves = not agents).
- **Concurrency reality here:** a Workflow runs **~min(16, cores−2) ≈ 10–14 at once** regardless; lifetime cap 1000. More than the concurrent cap just queues — so "10ish live" is the practical ceiling per graph.
- **Let the reorg rules set the count dynamically:** small task → **1** (run solo); unknown-size discovery → **loop-until-dry** (keep spawning until K rounds find nothing new); token target → `floor(budget/~100k)` workers; failure cluster → **+1 review board**. Count is decided at runtime, not up front.

So: don't pick a number — pick a **decomposition rule** + **reorg triggers**, and the graph sizes itself.

# Claude Code Plugin Anatomy — Reference

## 1. Plugin system layout on disk (`~/.claude/plugins/`)

```
~/.claude/plugins/
├── installed_plugins.json      # index of what's installed (schema v2)
├── known_marketplaces.json     # registered marketplaces → git source
├── plugin-catalog-cache.json   # 397KB cached browse catalog for /plugin
├── .last_inuse_sweep           # housekeeping timestamp
├── cache/<marketplace>/<plugin>/<version-or-sha>/   # ACTUAL installed plugin content
│   ├── caveman/caveman/25d22f864ad6/
│   └── openai-codex/codex/1.0.6/
├── marketplaces/<name>/        # full git clone of each marketplace repo
│   ├── caveman/
│   ├── openai-codex/
│   └── claude-plugins-official/
└── data/<plugin>-<marketplace>/  # per-plugin mutable runtime data (e.g. codex/state)
```

- `installed_plugins.json` (`~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json`): `{version:2, plugins:{ "caveman@caveman":[{scope:"user", installPath, version, installedAt, lastUpdated, gitCommitSha}] }}`. Key = `<plugin>@<marketplace>`; installPath points into `cache/`.
- `known_marketplaces.json`: `{ "caveman":{source:{source:"github", repo:"JuliusBrussee/caveman"}, installLocation, lastUpdated} }`. Marketplaces are just git repos.
- `cache/.../25d22f864ad6/` is a git checkout pinned to `gitCommitSha`; the directory name is the short sha (or a semver like `1.0.6` for codex).
- `.in_use/<pid>` files inside each cached plugin are live-session locks (PIDs).

## 2. Plugin manifest — `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` (REQUIRED)

Must live at `<plugin-root>/.claude-plugin/plugin.json`. Component dirs must be at plugin root, NOT inside `.claude-plugin/`.

Full field reference (from `~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/claude-plugins-official/plugins/plugin-dev/skills/plugin-structure/references/manifest-reference.md`):

| Field | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string (required) | kebab-case, unique, `^[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*$` |
| `version` | string | semver `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, default `0.1.0` |
| `description` | string | 50-200 chars |
| `author` | object or string | `{name, email?, url?}` |
| `homepage` | url | |
| `repository` | url or `{type,url,directory}` | |
| `license` | SPDX string | |
| `keywords` | string[] | |
| `commands` | string or string[] | extra command dirs, default `./commands`; must start `./`, no `../` |
| `agents` | string or string[] | extra agent dirs, default `./agents` |
| `hooks` | string (path) or inline object | default `./hooks/hooks.json` |
| `mcpServers` | string (path) or inline object | default `./.mcp.json` |

Component path fields SUPPLEMENT the default dirs (do not replace). Minimal valid manifest = `{"name":"x"}`.

Concrete caveman manifest (`.../25d22f864ad6/.claude-plugin/plugin.json`) declares only `name`, `description`, `author`, and inline `hooks` (SessionStart + UserPromptSubmit).

## 3. Component types + concrete formats

Auto-discovery scans: `commands/*.md`, `agents/*.md`, `skills/*/SKILL.md`, `hooks/hooks.json`, `.mcp.json`.

### Skills — `skills/<name>/SKILL.md`
YAML frontmatter + markdown body. Caveman example `.../skills/caveman/SKILL.md`:
```
---
name: caveman
description: >
  Ultra-compressed communication mode... Use when user says "caveman mode"...
---
<markdown instructions>
```
Frontmatter fields seen: `name`, `description` (the trigger text), optional `version`. Supporting files allowed in subdirs (`scripts/`, `references/`, `assets/`, `agents/`). Claude Code activates skills by matching `description`; they are also invokable as `/name` and namespaced `plugin:skill` (e.g. `caveman:caveman`). Skill dir MUST contain `SKILL.md` (README.md is ignored for discovery).

### Agents (subagents) — `agents/<name>.md`
Caveman example `.../agents/cavecrew-investigator.md`:
```
---
name: cavecrew-investigator
description: >
  Read-only code locator... Refuses to suggest fixes.
tools: [Read, Grep, Glob, Bash]
model: haiku
---
<system prompt body>
```
Fields: `name`, `description` (used for auto-delegation), `tools` (array or comma list), `model` (`haiku`/`sonnet`/`opus`), optional `skills:` list (codex example `.../openai-codex/.../agents/codex-rescue.md` has `model: sonnet`, `tools: Bash`, `skills: [codex-cli-runtime, gpt-5-4-prompting]`).

### Commands (slash commands) — `commands/<name>.md`
Markdown + frontmatter. `.../example-plugin/commands/example-command.md`:
```
---
description: An example slash command...
argument-hint: <required-arg> [optional-arg]
allowed-tools: [Read, Glob, Grep, Bash]
model: haiku            # optional override
---
Body. Uses $ARGUMENTS (and $1,$2). ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} available.
```
`<name>.md` → `/name`. codex `commands/rescue.md` shows `allowed-tools: Bash(node:*), AskUserQuestion, Agent` scoping.
**GOTCHA:** caveman's `commands/*.toml` (`description=`,`prompt=`) are NOT Claude Code commands — that's the Codex/Gemini format. Claude Code ignores them; caveman's `/caveman` etc. come from its **skills**. Do not copy the `.toml` shape for a Claude plugin.

### Hooks — inline in `plugin.json` OR `hooks/hooks.json`
Caveman inline (in plugin.json):
```json
"hooks": {
  "SessionStart": [{ "hooks": [{
    "type":"command",
    "command":"node \"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/src/hooks/caveman-activate.js\"",
    "timeout":5, "statusMessage":"Loading caveman mode..." }]}],
  "UserPromptSubmit": [{ "hooks":[{ "type":"command",
    "command":"node \"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/src/hooks/caveman-mode-tracker.js\"", "timeout":5 }]}]
}
```
External file form: codex `.../openai-codex/codex/1.0.6/hooks/hooks.json` (SessionStart, SessionEnd, Stop). Event types: `PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SubagentStop, SessionStart, SessionEnd, UserPromptSubmit, PreCompact, Notification`. `PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse` entries add a `"matcher":"Write|Edit"` (tool-name regex). Each hook: `{type:"command", command, timeout, statusMessage?}`. Scripts get stdin JSON + env incl. `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`, `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}`.

### MCP servers — `.mcp.json` at plugin root (or `mcpServers` in plugin.json)
Canonical `.mcp.json` (top-level keys = server names; NOT wrapped in `mcpServers`). `.../example-plugin/.mcp.json`:
```json
{ "example-server": { "type":"http", "url":"https://mcp.example.com/api" } }
```
Types + shapes (`plugin-dev/skills/mcp-integration/examples/*.json`):
- stdio: `{"command":"node","args":["${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/servers/x.js"],"env":{"K":"${K}"}}`
- http: `{"type":"http","url":"...","headers":{"Authorization":"Bearer ${TOKEN}"}}`
- sse: `{"type":"sse","url":"https://mcp.asana.com/sse"}` (OAuth auto)
- ws: `{"type":"ws","url":"wss://...","headers":{...}}`

Inline-in-manifest form wraps under `"mcpServers": {...}`. Servers auto-start on plugin enable. Tool names become `mcp__plugin_<plugin-name>_<server-name>__<tool-name>`; pre-allow in command/agent frontmatter `allowed-tools`. Real external `.mcp.json` examples: `.../claude-plugins-official/external_plugins/{context7,linear,playwright,github,...}/.mcp.json`.
**Caveman deviation:** caveman ships an MCP server `src/mcp-servers/caveman-shrink/` (a prose-compression stdio proxy, `bin: index.js`) but does NOT declare it in `plugin.json`. Its installer (`bin/install.js`, opt-in `--with-mcp-shrink`) writes it into the user's `settings.json`/`opencode.json` `mcp` block instead. So it's not the plugin-native path — use `.mcp.json` for a new plugin.

### Statusline
No `statusLine` field in the plugin manifest schema. Caveman provides `src/hooks/caveman-statusline.sh` / `.ps1` and its installer writes a `settings.json` `statusLine: {command: "bash .../caveman-statusline.sh"}` entry (`bin/install.js` ~L896, `bin/lib/settings.js` L280-285). Statusline is a user-`settings.json` feature, wired by an installer script, not auto-discovered from the manifest.

## 4. Distribution / installation

A **marketplace** = a git repo with `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` at its root. Plugins are installed via `/plugin` (marketplace browse) or `claude plugin` CLI, which clones the marketplace into `~/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/<name>/` and checks the plugin out into `cache/`.

`marketplace.json` schema (`.../claude-plugins-official/.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`):
```json
{
  "$schema":"https://anthropic.com/claude-code/marketplace.schema.json",
  "name":"...", "description":"...",
  "owner":{"name":"...","email":"..."},
  "renames":{ "old":"new" },              // optional alias map
  "plugins":[ { "name","description","author","category","homepage",
    "source": <see below> } ]
}
```
`source` variants observed:
- `"./"` or `"./plugins/agent-sdk-dev"` — plugin lives in this same repo (relative path). Caveman uses `"source":"./"` (repo root IS the plugin).
- `{"source":"git-subdir","url":"https://github.com/.../x.git","path":"plugins/...","ref":"v1.5.5","sha":"..."}` — external git repo, pinned.

Single-repo plugin (caveman) can be BOTH a plugin and a 1-entry marketplace: repo root has `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` AND `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` (`plugins:[{name:"caveman", source:"./", category:"productivity"}]`). Others install it by adding the marketplace `github:JuliusBrussee/caveman` then installing `caveman`. (Caveman also ships a `curl … install.sh` path and multi-runtime targets `.codex/`, `gemini-extension.json`, `src/plugins/opencode/` — ignore those for a pure Claude plugin.)

Authoring scaffold references live in the official `plugin-dev` plugin: `.../claude-plugins-official/plugins/plugin-dev/skills/{plugin-structure,command-development,agent-development,hook-development,skill-development,mcp-integration,plugin-settings}/` — each has `SKILL.md`, `references/`, `examples/`. `plugin-structure/examples/{minimal,standard,advanced}-plugin.md` are copy-ready layouts.

## 5. Workflows (NOT a plugin component — clarification)

`.claude/workflows/` under a plugin does not exist. The workflow files found live per-session at `~/.claude/projects/<proj-slug>/<session-id>/workflows/`:
```
workflows/
├── wf_<id>.json                       # run record: {runId,taskId,script,scriptPath,result,phases,agents,tokens,...}
└── scripts/<name>-wf_<id>.js          # the executed workflow script
```
This is the Claude Code SDK **Workflow tool** (session-scoped orchestration), not a plugin distribution artifact. Script format (`.js`):
```js
export const meta = { name, description, phases:[{title,detail}] }
phase('Understand')
const raw = await parallel(readers.map(r => () => agent(r.prompt, {label, phase, model:'sonnet', effort:'high'})))
phase('Synthesize')
const out = await agent(prompt, {label, phase, effort:'high'})
return out
```
Globals available in a workflow script: `phase()`, `agent(prompt, opts)`, `parallel([fns])`, `export const meta`. A **skill cannot "declare" a workflow**; a SKILL.md is plain markdown and can only instruct the model to invoke the Workflow tool at runtime (write such a `.js`). There is no manifest field binding skills→workflows.

## 6. Canonical layout to author a new plugin

```
my-plugin/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   ├── plugin.json          # {name, version, description, author, ...}
│   └── marketplace.json     # only if repo doubles as its own marketplace
├── commands/<name>.md       # slash commands (md + frontmatter)
├── agents/<name>.md         # subagents (md + frontmatter: name/description/tools/model)
├── skills/<name>/SKILL.md   # skills (+ scripts/ references/ assets/)
├── hooks/hooks.json         # or inline "hooks" in plugin.json
├── .mcp.json                # MCP servers (or inline "mcpServers")
├── scripts/                 # helper scripts, referenced via ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}
├── LICENSE
└── README.md
```
Rules: manifest in `.claude-plugin/` only; components at root only; kebab-case names; always reference intra-plugin paths with `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` (never absolute/`~`/cwd-relative); component-path fields in the manifest must start with `./`.</result>

# Plan: "Graph Loop" plugin — self-prompting agent org wired to entire graph + brain

## Context (why)
The user wants to package the "dynamic agent org / self-prompting graph loop" pattern (loops→graphs; the UNWIND-AI operating-graph image) as a **distributable plugin others can install**, with **entire graph (`entire sem`)** and **entire brain** built in as the code-intelligence + durable-shared-state layer. Turn the orchestration they've been running ad-hoc (fan-out audits, comprehension workflows) into a reusable, installable plugin: agents = compute, brain/files = shared state, `entire graph` = the code graph, metrics close the loop, the graph reorganizes itself at runtime, and each run improves the next via brain distill.

## Grounding (from exploration — verified)
**Claude Code plugin anatomy** (model: the caveman plugin):
- Manifest `<<root>>/.claude-plugin/plugin.json` (only `name` required; +version/description/author, and component-dir/`mcpServers`/`hooks` fields).
- Components at plugin root: `agents/<name>.md` (frontmatter `name`/`description`/`tools`/`model` + system-prompt body), `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (frontmatter `name`/`description` trigger + markdown; supporting `scripts/`,`references/`,`assets/`), `commands/<name>.md` (`/name`, `$ARGUMENTS`, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`), `hooks/hooks.json` (SessionStart/SessionEnd/etc.), `.mcp.json` (server decls).
- **MCP decl to embed brain** (`.mcp.json`, top-level keys = server names): `{"entire-brain":{"type":"stdio","command":"entire","args":["brain","mcp"]}}`. Tool names surface as `mcp__plugin_<plugin>_entire-brain__brain_*`; pre-allow in agent/command `allowed-tools`.
- Distribution: a **marketplace** = git repo with `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`; a single repo can be BOTH the plugin and a 1-entry marketplace (caveman does `source:"./"`). Install: add marketplace `github:owner/repo` → `/plugin install`.
- **Workflows are NOT an auto-discovered component**, but a plugin may ship `workflows/*.js` as assets; a skill/command instructs the model to run them via the Workflow tool with `{scriptPath}` (official `code-modernization` plugin pattern). Script DSL: `export const meta`, `phase()`, `agent(prompt,{label,phase,model,effort,schema,agentType})`, `parallel()`, `pipeline()`, `budget`.

**entire graph + brain integration** (both **local, no egress** by default):
- Brain MCP: `entire brain mcp` (stdio JSON-RPC). Tools: `brain_status/brief/query/search/vsearch/get/multi_get/context/impact/code/search_graph/query_graph/trace_path/regressions/review/patterns/tests/…` + local mutating `brain_index_repository`. Env: `ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT` binds the repo.
- Code graph: `entire graph snapshot|symbols|edges|diff|search --format ndjson` (provider `entire-graph`, `no_egress:true`). Brain shells out to it to build the semantic layer.
- Third-party prereqs: the `entire` CLI on PATH + the `graph`(cgo/tree-sitter) and `brain`(pure-Go, offline embeddings) Entire plugins installed (`entire plugin install` / `scripts/install.sh`). Login only needed for hosted/shared brain + session capture — **local build works offline** (`entire brain refresh` → `entire brain status`; optional `entire brain distill` for facts).
- Two ecosystems exist: **Entire plugins** (`entire-plugin.yml`, `requires:`) vs **Claude Code plugins** (this plan's default target).

**Reuse, don't reinvent:** skills `deep-research` (fan-out→verify→synthesize), `loop`/`schedule` (self-prompting recurrence), `audit` (convergence-until-clean); agent-seat `.md` shape from cavecrew + feature-dev; user's `orchestrator-architecture.md` doctrine (delegation tiers, isolated worktrees, live-verify, no AI footers) + `self-improvement-loop.md` (brain distill closes the loop).

## Proposed architecture (Claude Code plugin: working name `graph-loop`)
```
graph-loop/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   ├── plugin.json           # name, version, description, author, mcpServers→.mcp.json
│   └── marketplace.json      # self-marketplace (source:"./") so `github:owner/graph-loop` installs it
├── .mcp.json                 # {"entire-brain":{stdio, command:"entire", args:["brain","mcp"]}}
├── skills/
│   └── graph-loop/SKILL.md   # the loops→graphs doctrine + when-to-use + "run the bundled workflow via Workflow tool"; runtime-reorg rules; brain/graph usage contract
├── commands/
│   └── graph-loop.md         # /graph-loop <goal> — entry point; preflight then invoke the workflow
├── agents/                   # the org "seats" (contract-driven, cavecrew-style)
│   ├── gl-control.md         # control plane / org designer: reads brain+state, emits the round's plan (schema)
│   ├── gl-research.md        # research/explore seat: uses `entire graph` + brain_search/context, file:line evidence
│   ├── gl-build.md           # build/implement seat (isolated worktree; live-verify doctrine)
│   ├── gl-critic.md          # adversarial verify/critic seat (confirm-or-refute, concrete failing input)
│   └── gl-measure.md         # measure seat: computes metrics, writes them back to shared state
├── workflows/
│   └── graph-loop.js         # runnable self-prompting graph: plan→parallel(seats)→measure→merge-to-state→reorg→loop-until-goal/dry/budget
├── hooks/hooks.json          # SessionStart: preflight (entire present? brain indexed?). SessionEnd: `entire brain refresh` to close the improvement loop (opt-in)
├── scripts/
│   └── preflight.sh          # checks `entire`, graph+brain plugins, brain_status; prints install hints; degrades gracefully if absent
├── README.md  LICENSE
```
**How the pieces realize the image:** `gl-control` = MONICA (org designer); `gl-research`/`gl-build` = DWIGHT/ROSS; **SHARED STATE** = brain (`brain_*`) + a run state file every seat reads/writes; `entire graph` = the code-graph substrate; `gl-measure` = AUDIENCE SIGNALS (metrics→state); **runtime reorg** = conditionals in `graph-loop.js` (small task→run solo; failure cluster→add critic; budget>progress→collapse fan-out; 2× fix→promote model); **self-prompting** = `gl-control` composes round N+1's prompts from state+metrics; **self-improvement** = SessionEnd `entire brain refresh`/`distill` turns runs into durable facts the next run recalls.

## Open decisions (need user input — see AskUserQuestion)
1. Distribution ecosystem: Claude Code plugin vs Entire plugin vs hybrid.
2. Brain/graph posture for third parties: local-only (no login) vs hosted/shared (login) vs optional graceful-degrade.
3. v1 scope: full org + reorg + self-improvement vs a lean MVP (one skill + one workflow + brain MCP + preflight).

## Verification (to fill after decisions)
- `claude plugin` install from a scratch marketplace clone → `/graph-loop <goal>` runs end-to-end.
- Preflight correctly detects missing `entire`/brain and prints install hints; brain MCP tools resolve (`mcp__plugin_graph-loop_entire-brain__brain_status`).
- The workflow completes a full plan→fan-out→measure→reorg→loop cycle on a toy goal; brain read+write verified via `entire brain status`.

content.text:
Sure — what would you like to clarify? Happy to reframe.

To help, here's what's behind each question:

- **Ecosystem** — where it installs from. *Claude Code plugin* = any CC user adds a git marketplace + `/plugin install` (like caveman). *Entire plugin* = only `entire` CLI users, `entire loop <goal>`. *Hybrid* = CC plugin that also pulls in the entire brain/graph plugins.
- **Brain posture** — how third parties get memory + code graph. *Local-only* = works offline, no login (just install `entire`). *Hosted* = shared team brain, needs login + cloud. *Optional* = plugin still runs if they don't have `entire`, just without graph/memory.
- **v1 scope** — how much to build first. *Full* = all 5 agent seats + runtime reorg + self-improvement distill. *MVP* = one skill + one workflow + brain wiring, iterate after.

What's unclear, or what other context/constraints should I fold in? (e.g. who the audience is, whether it must work without the entire CLI, a name, or whether you want it as an Entire-org thing vs a public open-source plugin.)
explain trade offs

## 1. Ecosystem — where it lives / who can install

| Option | Wins | Costs |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code plugin** | Any CC user installs via git marketplace (1 step). Native fit: skills/agents/workflows/MCP already the graph-loop's shape. Brain wires in via `.mcp.json` one-liner. Public-shareable like caveman. | Still needs `entire` CLI present for brain/graph to actually work (MCP `command:"entire"`). So "installed" ≠ "functional" unless they also have entire. |
| **Entire plugin** | Tightest coupling — `requires: [graph, brain]` guarantees deps; brain/graph are already Entire plugins. `entire loop <goal>` feels native. | Reach limited to `entire` CLI users only. You write Go (`cmd/entire-loop`), not just markdown. No CC skill/subagent ergonomics — you'd reimplement orchestration the harness gives free. |
| **Hybrid** | Max capability: CC ergonomics + guaranteed brain/graph. | Two install steps (CC marketplace + `entire plugin install`). Most moving parts to maintain + document. Highest support burden. |

**Lean:** Claude Code plugin. The graph-loop IS skills+agents+workflow — building it as Go in the Entire ecosystem throws away the harness orchestration you'd otherwise get free.

## 2. Brain posture — how hard the dependency

| Option | Wins | Costs |
|---|---|---|
| **Local-only, no login** | Works offline, zero cloud, zero auth friction. Anyone who installs `entire` gets full graph + durable memory. Privacy: nothing leaves the machine (`no_egress:true`). | Memory is per-machine — no team sharing. Each user builds their own brain (`entire brain refresh`). |
| **Hosted / shared brain** | Team shares one brain — collective memory across people/machines. | Needs `entire login` + entire-api + egress. Auth failures (401/403) become support tickets. Not usable air-gapped. Ties the plugin to Entire cloud availability. |
| **Optional / degrade** | Runs even with no `entire` at all — widest install base, lowest barrier. | The default experience is gutted: no real code graph, no memory — just plain fan-out/verify (which `deep-research` already does). The whole "entire graph + brain" value is the thing that's optional. |

**Lean:** Local-only as the default, with hosted as a config flag later. Degrade-gracefully is worth adding *on top* (so a no-`entire` user still gets a working loop), but not as the primary mode — else the brain/graph selling point is optional.

Note: these two questions interact — a **CC plugin + local-only brain** gives the best reach-without-cloud combo. Hosted only makes sense if the audience is an Entire team.

## 3. v1 scope — how much first

| Option | Wins | Costs |
|---|---|---|
| **Full org + self-improvement** | Delivers the image: 5 seats + runtime reorg + self-prompting + brain-distill improvement loop. Impressive, complete. | Bigger surface = more to get right + debug. Reorg rules + distill loop are the parts most likely to need iteration. Slower to first working install. |
| **Lean MVP** | Fast to a *working, installable* plugin: proves the marketplace install + brain MCP wiring + one plan→fan-out→verify→synthesize loop. De-risks the plumbing before the fancy parts. | Not yet the self-rewriting org — reorg + distill come in v2. Reads as "another fan-out tool" until then. |

**Lean:** MVP first, but scoped so the full org is a clean extension (same seats/workflow file, add reorg conditionals + SessionEnd distill in v2). Ship the skeleton that installs + wires brain, then layer the self-improvement.

## The interactions that matter
- **Reach vs. power:** CC-plugin + optional-degrade = max reach, min power. CC-plugin + local-only = the sweet spot (works for anyone with `entire`, full power, no cloud). Entire-plugin + hosted = a team-internal tool.
- **Support burden** scales with cloud (hosted brain = auth tickets) and install steps (hybrid = 2 installs).
- **Time-to-first-demo:** MVP + CC + local-only is fastest to something you can install and show.

My default recommendation across all three: **Claude Code plugin · local-only brain (degrade-gracefully as a bonus) · MVP first, full org in v2.** Want me to lock that in, or pick differently on any axis?

## entire-judge — LLM-invocation, auth, and cloud analysis

**On disk.** `/Users/suhaan/Documents/Coding/entire-judge/` (git remote `https://github.com/entireio/entire-judge.git`; go module namespaced as `github.com/suhaanthayyil/entire-judge`). ### Structure as an Entire plugin
- **No `entire-plugin.yml` exists** (not on disk, not git-tracked). It is an "external-command" plugin: a Cobra binary named `entire-judge` that the parent CLI dispatches on `entire judge`. Registration is `entire plugin install ./entire-judge --force` (README:38-53), which drops the symlink into the managed `bin/`. So "requires / egress / permissions" are not declared in a manifest — egress policy is enforced in Go code (see below).
- **Entrypoint:** `cmd/entire-judge/main.go` → `cli.Execute(version, os.Args[1:])` → `internal/cli/root.go:46 NewRootCommand`.
- **Command tree** (`root.go:77-81`): `add`, `run`, `rank`, `watch`, `version`. LLM lens flags registered at `root.go:121-129`: `--agent` (default `claude-code`), `--model`, `--effort`, `--jobs` (concurrent scoring, default 4).
- **Host contract via env only** (`internal/cli/env.go:14-16`): `ENTIRE_CLI_VERSION`, `ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT`, `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR`.

### How it drives the LLM — pattern (b): shells out to an agent CLI
No Go SDK, no gateway. It builds an argv and execs a local agent CLI, feeding the system prompt as a positional arg and the brief on **stdin**.

Raw `os/exec` — **no helper, no SDK**. brain defines its own `CommandRunner` / `CommandStreamer` interfaces and an `ExecRunner` that wraps `exec.CommandContext` (`/Users/suhaan/Documents/Coding/entire-brain/internal/cli/runner.go`). `/Users/suhaan/Documents/Coding/entire-brain/internal/cli/semantic_stream.go` (`streamSemanticSnapshot`):

# Plan: `entire-loop` — a self-prompting agent-org plugin wired to entire graph + brain ## Context (why) Package the "dynamic agent org / self-prompting graph loop" pattern (loops→graphs; the UNWIND-AI operating-graph image) as a **distributable Entire plugin** others install, with **entire graph (`entire sem`)** + **entire brain** built in as the code-intelligence + durable-shared-state layer. ` / `codex exec …` / loopback `ollama` (`entire-judge/internal/agent/agent.go:47`, exec `runner.go:39`). `brain-swebench`: `claude -p "" --model M --output-format json --dangerously-skip-permissions --max-turns N` → JSON envelope `{total_cost_usd,is_error,result,num_turns,usage}` (`run_cc_one.sh:185`). Each accepted round makes the next run more capable = the self-improvement loop, literal. 4. No auto-merge, no hot-swap of the running binary.

27	// binds the entire-brain stdio server for deep seats.

# Adversarial audit — `entire-loop` (READ-ONLY)

**Build/vet/test:** `go build ./...` clean · `go vet ./...` clean · `go test ./...` 58 pass · `go test -race ./...` 58 pass.
**Critical coverage gap:** every test mocks the runner (`FakeRunner`). `internal/agent/spawn.go` (`runWithReaping` — the entire process-group reaping/timeout path) is **never exercised by any test, including `-race`**. No real `claude` is ever spawned. All PASS-A process findings below are in code the suite never runs.

---

## CONFIRMED

**[crit] cmd/entire-loop/main.go:20 + internal/cli/root.go:32 + internal/cli/commands.go:101 — no signal→context wiring, so interrupts orphan every worker + grandchild.**
`main` calls `cli.Execute` → `cmd.Execute()` (not `ExecuteContext`), so `cmd.Context()` is `context.Background()` and is **never cancelled**. Combined with `Setpgid=true` (spawn.go:32) this is the worst case: each `claude` runs in its *own* process group, so a terminal Ctrl-C (SIGINT to the *foreground* group = orchestrator only) does **not** reach the workers. The orchestrator dies on default SIGINT; `runWithReaping`'s group-kill only fires on `ctx.Done()`, which never happens. Result: orchestrator exits, `claude` + its `node`/MCP grandchildren keep running as orphans, burning API credit until they finish on their own.
Scenario: `entire loop run "…" --rounds 3`, two seats mid-flight, press Ctrl-C → shell returns, but `ps` still shows `claude`/`node` alive.
Fix: `ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM); defer stop()` and `root.ExecuteContext(ctx)`. The reaping code is correct; it just never gets the cancel.

**[high] internal/context/brief.go:76-77,101,116-124,172-173 — brief sibling shell-outs have NO timeout; a hung `entire graph`/`entire brain` hangs the whole loop.** `defaultExec` = `exec.CommandContext(ctx, …).Output()` using the loop's ambient ctx, which carries no deadline (per-worker timeout is applied only around the `claude` spawn in runner.go, not around brief building). If `entire graph symbols` or `entire brain context` hangs, `Brief` blocks → the seat goroutine blocks → `wg.Wait()` (loop.go:154) never returns → the round and the whole run hang forever. `gatherBrainContext` never reaches its `brain query` fallback if `brain context` *hangs* (fallback only triggers on error, brief.go:117).
Scenario: `entire brain context` deadlocks on a cold index; `entire loop run` hangs indefinitely with no output.
Fix: wrap each sibling call in its own `context.WithTimeout` (e.g. 15-30s, mirroring `probeTimeout` already defined in commands.go:23).

**[high] internal/context/brief.go:173,101,105 — unbounded memory: full `entire graph symbols` stream buffered before truncation.** `.Output()` reads *all* of stdout into memory; only afterward does `gatherGraph` `strings.Split` and take `headLines` (200). On a large monorepo the ndjson symbol dump (hundreds of MB) is fully materialized (plus the `Split` slice) before being thrown away. The 256KiB `MaxOutputBytes` cap applies only to the *worker's* stdout in `runWithReaping`, not to brief siblings.
Scenario: target repo with a huge symbol graph → orchestrator RSS spikes to hundreds of MB / OOM per brief, ×seats.
Fix: stream the command's stdout through a line-bounded reader (cap at `headLines`/`sectionCap`) instead of `.Output()`.

**[med] internal/agent/parse.go:171-190 (stripJSONFences) → 71 — a valid seat object containing a ```` ``` ```` sequence is destroyed, losing the whole result.** `stripJSONFences` blindly slices between the first and next `` ``` `` with zero JSON awareness, running *before* the brace-balanced extractor. **Empirically confirmed:** input `{"proposal":"run ```json``` then stop","verdict":"ok"}` → strip yields `"json"` → `extractOuterJSONObject` returns `("",false)` → "seat output contained no JSON object", `OK=false`. A critic/build seat that quotes a fenced code block in its proposal silently degrades to a failed seat.
Fix: only strip a fence when the object doesn't parse as-is, or run the balanced extractor first and fall back to fence-stripping; don't slice on the *first* backtick unconditionally.

**[med] internal/agent/seats.go:99-101 + runner.go:70-74 — deep seat with empty RepoRoot binds the brain to the orchestrator's cwd, silently.** When `McpBrain=true` but `spec.RepoRoot==""` (only when `r.RepoRoot==""` too, since runner.go:61-63 backfills), `cmd.Env` stays `nil` → child inherits the orchestrator's *full* env, and `cmd.Dir` also stays unset (runner.go:70-74 sets Dir only if `r.Dir`/`r.RepoRoot` non-empty) → `claude` and thus `entire brain mcp` run in the orchestrator's cwd with no `ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT` → brain binds the **wrong repo**, no warning. The CLI mitigates this (`resolveRepoRoot` errors out if it can't resolve, so RepoRoot is non-empty in practice), but the agent package is defensively broken for any library/test caller, and there's no guard/warning.
Fix: if `McpBrain && RepoRoot==""`, either return a warning-degraded result or refuse; at minimum always set `cmd.Dir` and never leave a brain seat's repo ambient.

**[low] internal/templates/templates.go:50-55 — marker substitution is order-dependent and injectable, so briefs are nondeterministic.** `Render` iterates `values` in Go's randomized map order and does successive `ReplaceAll`. **Empirically confirmed:** when a value contains a literal marker (e.g. goal text `"do X ${METRICS} Y"`), output varies run-to-run (2 distinct results over 2000 renders — 1757 vs 243). A goal or graph line containing `${METRICS}`/`${GRAPH}` gets substituted or blanked unpredictably.
Fix: single-pass replacement over a fixed marker order using `strings.NewReplacer` (which does non-overlapping left-to-right replacement and won't re-expand injected markers).

**[low] internal/context/brief.go:176-184 (boundString) — 64KiB cap slices on a byte boundary, can emit invalid UTF-8 (no panic).** **Empirically confirmed:** `s[:max-3]` landing mid-rune yields a dangling `\xc3` (`utf8.ValidString==false`). No panic (Go string slicing is byte-indexed and safe — so the task's "panic slicing a rune" concern is a non-issue), but the brief's final rune can be corrupt. Applies to every `truncate`/`boundString` call, incl. the section caps.
Fix: back up to a rune boundary (`for !utf8.RuneStart(s[i])`) before slicing.

**[low] internal/agent/runner.go:111-124 (saveCached) — seat cache write is non-atomic (unlike state.Save).** `os.WriteFile` (truncate-in-place), not tmp+rename. A crash mid-write leaves a truncated `seats/<role>.json`; `loadCached` (json.Unmarshal) fails → returns `(_,false)` → re-runs, so it self-heals for the single-writer MVP. But it's inconsistent with `state.Store.Save`'s atomic pattern and would corrupt under Phase-B duplicate-role plans (two same-role seats → concurrent `os.WriteFile` to one path).
Fix: reuse the tmp+rename pattern from store.go:128-145; assert unique roles in the planner.

---

## POSSIBLE / minor

**[low] internal/agent/spawn.go:44-45 — a leaked grandchild holding the stdout pipe delays `cmd.Wait()` up to the full 20-min worker timeout even on fast success.** Because `cmd.Stdout` is a non-`*os.File`, `os/exec` spawns copy goroutines that `Wait()` joins; they only finish when *every* fd holding the pipe closes. If `claude` exits fast but a backgrounded `node`/MCP inherits and holds stdout, `done` never fires on the success path, so `runWithReaping` blocks until the `DefaultWorkerTimeout` (1200s) fires and SIGKILLs the group. Correctness is preserved (timeout reaps it) but a 10-second seat can stall 20 minutes. Not test-covered. Fix: give the child an explicit `os.Pipe` you own and stop reading on process exit, or set a shorter idle deadline.

**[nit] internal/agent/spawn.go:55 — `time.After(killGrace)` timer isn't stopped when the process dies during grace.** If `<-done` wins the inner select, the 5s timer lives until it fires. Bounded, per-timeout-event; use `t := time.NewTimer; defer t.Stop()`.

**[nit] internal/cli/commands.go:130-132 — runID = `<UTC-seconds>-<pid>` can theoretically collide.** Two runs need the same pid within the same wall-clock second; effectively impossible for a single-shot CLI (each invocation is a distinct pid), and separate invocations get distinct pids. Practically safe; add sub-second/random suffix if ever run in-process.

**[info] no-egress advertises ollama but can't use it.** `RejectForNoEgress` (egress.go:32-39) permits `ollama`, but `BuildCmd` (seats.go:95) hardcodes `"claude"` — nothing ever spawns a local model. Under `ENTIRE_BRAIN_NO_EGRESS`, `runLoop` correctly fails fast (commands.go:63) *before* building briefs, so this is a clean refusal, not a hang. Just note the ollama branch is currently dead.

---

## What's solid

- **Process-group reaping mechanics** (spawn.go): `Setpgid` set *before* `Start`; `pgid = cmd.Process.Pid` correct with `Pgid=0`; whole group signalled via `syscall.Kill(-pgid, …)`; SIGTERM→5s grace→SIGKILL; the `done` goroutine can't leak (buffered cap-1, drained on every path); no data race on `cappedBuffer` (always read after `<-done`, i.e. after `Wait` joins the copiers — race detector agrees, though it never actually runs this path). The bug is *reaching* this code on interrupt, not the code itself.
- **Per-worker timeout** is genuinely applied (`context.WithTimeout` in runWithReaping); parent-ctx cancellation *does* propagate and reap the tree — the gap is purely that the ctx is never cancelled (crit finding above).
- **`extractOuterJSONObject`** correctly handles braces-in-strings, escaped quotes, nested objects, no-JSON (`false`), unbalanced (`false`), and is byte-safe for valid UTF-8 (`{`,`}`,`"`,`\` never appear as UTF-8 continuation bytes). "First object only" on multi-object input is documented/intended.
- **Egress gate** is not bypassable: `ExecRunner.Run` calls `RejectForNoEgress` first (before cache load and before any spawn), the only spawn path routes through it, and the CLI double-gates at entry. `envBool` truthy parsing (`1/true/yes/on`, trimmed, case-insensitive) is correct.
- **Loop termination**: no off-by-one — fresh run does exactly `Rounds` rounds (`start=st.Round+1`, `round<=Rounds`); resume is correct; a completed run runs zero rounds; cannot infinite-loop or under-run; all-seats-fail terminates cleanly and persists state every round.
- **Concurrency**: `fanOut` semaphore is bounded and deadlock-free (each acquire matched by exactly one deferred release); results written to disjoint indices (no race); per-seat errors are isolated (Runner never returns error; one failed seat doesn't abort the round); `st` is only read during fan-out and mutated afterward, so concurrent brief reads are safe.
- **state.Store.Save** is properly atomic (CreateTemp in same dir + Rename) and single-writer (only the main loop goroutine writes `state.json`; seats write only their own cache files). Missing `fsync` on file+dir is a durability nit, not a corruption risk.</result>

maek the mvp build it self; more info;Graph Engineering with Claude: 14-Step roadmap from 0 to graph architect (Full Course)
Most people who try to build a multi-step agent end up with a straight line. Step one, step two, step three - each waiting politely for the last to finish before it starts.
9/10 notice that half those steps never needed to wait at all.
They don’t route. They don’t branch. They don’t parallelize. They just queue - one head, one context, one thing at a time, until the window fills up and the agent forgets what it was doing.
Follow my Substack to get fresh AI alpha: movez.substack.com
This is the 14-step roadmap that turns that single-file line into a graph: one that fans out across a fleet, verifies its own findings, and converges on a result a lone agent could never hold.
Here’s the shift nobody spells out. A prompt is a sentence. A loop is a cycle. A harness is the floor the agent stands on. 
But the shape of the work itself - what runs before what, what can run at the same time, what has to wait for everything else - that shape is a graph. Nodes do the thinking. Edges carry the results. 
Claude Code shipped the tooling to build these graphs directly: dynamic workflows. 
Claude writes a plain JavaScript orchestration script, then spawns a coordinated fleet of subagents to execute it - and the coordination itself costs zero model tokens, because it’s code, not a conversation.

01. Nodes are jobs. Edges are what flows.
A graph has exactly two things, and getting them straight fixes most of the confusion. A node is a unit of work - one agent, one bounded job, one input in and one output out. 
An edge is a dependency: it says this node’s output feeds that node’s input. Nothing more.
The mistake is treating “and then” as an edge. “Summarize the file and then tell me the weather” has no edge between the two - the weather doesn’t consume the summary. 
That’s two disconnected nodes that a linear script needlessly chains. The edge only exists when data actually moves across it. 
Learn to ask, for every “and then” in your agent: does the next step read the last step’s output? If not, there is no edge, and the wait is wasted.
python
Draw it as boxes and arrows. A box is an agent() call. 
An arrow is a variable passed from one call’s return into another’s 
prompt. If you can’t draw the arrow - if no variable crosses - the two 
boxes are independent, and independence is the thing you’ll exploit 
for the rest of this course.

02. Your linear script is a degenerate graph
When you write an agent as “do A, then B, then C, then D,” you’ve drawn a graph - a single unbranching chain. Every node has exactly one edge in and one edge out.
 It runs correctly. It also runs slowly and fragile, because a chain has no redundancy: if C stalls, D never happens, and A’s work is trapped upstream with nowhere to go.
The first real skill of graph engineering is redrawing the chain. Take your linear agent and, for each arrow, ask the Step 1 question. 
Most chains have two or three arrows that don’t carry data - they’re just the order you happened to type things in. 
Cut those arrows and the chain collapses into something wider: a few independent nodes that could all run at once, feeding a single node that needs them all.

03. Give every node a contract
A node you can’t reason about is a node you can’t parallelize. The fix is a contract: bounded input, bounded output, exactly one job. 
The input is whatever the node reads - passed in explicitly, never assumed from a shared window. The output is a defined shape, ideally validated, so the next node can consume it without guessing.
In a workflow this contract is enforced with a schema. When you hand Claude an agent() call with a JSON schema, the subagent Claude spawns is forced to return validated structured data - validation happens at the tool-call layer, so Claude retries on mismatch instead of handing you free text you have to parse and pray over. 
This is the difference between a node Claude can wire into a graph and a node that only works when a human reads its output.
python
// A node with a real contract: bounded in, validated out, one job.
const ITEM = {
  type: 'object', additionalProperties: false,
  properties: {
    title:   { type: 'string' },
    url:     { type: 'string' },
    impact:  { type: 'string', enum: ['high', 'medium', 'low'] },
  },
  required: ['title', 'url', 'impact'],
};

const result = await agent(source.prompt, {
  label:  `research:${source.key}`,
  schema: ITEM,           // forces validated structured output
  agentType: 'general-purpose',
});
// result is now a shape the next node can trust — not free text.

04. Treat the edge as a data contract
An edge isn’t just “B comes after A.” It’s a promise about what crosses: A produces this shape, and B is built to consume this shape. When you name the edge by its data - not its order - two things get easier. 
You can see instantly whether the edge is real (does data actually move?), and you can swap the node on either end without breaking the graph, as long as the shape holds.
In practice, the edge lives in plain JavaScript. The reduce step between fan-out and synthesis - flatten, dedupe, filter - is just code operating on the shapes your nodes returned. 
No agent needed. One of the quiet wins of graph thinking: a huge amount of what people burn model tokens on is really an edge, and edges are free.
python
The temptation is to spawn an agent to “combine the results.” Resist 
it. If combining means flatten-and-dedupe, that’s results.flatMap(...) 
and a Set — deterministic, instant, zero tokens. Save agents for 
judgment, not for plumbing. A graph where every edge is an agent is a 
graph paying rent on its own wiring.

05. Fan out with parallel()
This is the move that pays for everything. When you have N independent nodes - N sources to check, N files to review, N routes to audit - you don’t chain them. 
You tell Claude to fan them out and run them at once. In a workflow that’s parallel(): Claude takes an array of thunks and spawns one subagent per thunk, all executing concurrently, then hands you back the array of results.
Two details make it robust. First, parallel() is a barrier - it waits for every thunk before it returns, so the next stage sees the complete set. Second, a thunk that throws resolves to null instead of rejecting the whole batch, so one flaky agent can’t sink the run. 
Always .filter(Boolean) the results. Concurrency is capped around your core count and the excess queues, so you can pass a hundred thunks and they’ll all finish - just a handful at a time.
python
phase('Research');

// Nine sources, nine agents, all at once.
const raw = await parallel(
  SOURCES.map((s) => () =>
    agent(s.prompt, {
      label: `research:${s.key}`,
      phase: 'Research',
      schema: ITEM_SCHEMA,     // each node returns validated JSON
      agentType: 'general-purpose',
    }),
  ),
);

const collected = raw.filter(Boolean);  // drop the nulls from failed agents
The fan-out lives in code Claude wrote, not in a model conversation. Claude’s own context never holds nine sources at once - each subagent carries its own, and only the final answer comes back. 
That’s what lets Claude scale a workflow to dozens or hundreds of subagents without drowning the session. The orchestration layer costs zero tokens because it isn’t another turn of Claude thinking.

06. Fan in at a barrier
A fan-out is only useful if something gathers it. The fan-in is the node where edges converge - where one agent (or one piece of code) sees all the upstream results at once and does something that requires the whole set: dedupe across sources, rank by impact, early-exit if the total came back empty. This is the one place a barrier earns its wall-clock cost.
The rule that keeps graphs fast: use a barrier only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together. Deduping across all sources? Barrier - correct. 
python
// The edge: plain JS, no agent, zero tokens.
const flat = collected.flatMap((c) => c.items);
log(`Collected ${flat.length} items`);

phase('Curate');
// The barrier node: needs the WHOLE set to dedupe + rank.
const curated = await agent(
  `Dedupe and rank these by impact:\n${JSON.stringify(flat)}`,
  { phase: 'Curate', schema: CURATED_SCHEMA },
);
Just flattening a list? That’s an edge, do it inline. The smell test is brutal and simple: if you wrote parallel → transform → parallel, and that middle transform has no cross-item dependency, you should have used a pipeline and skipped the barrier entirely.

07. The diamond: split → work → merge
Put fan-out and fan-in together and you get the workhorse topology of every serious agent graph: the diamond.
 One node splits the job, many nodes do the work in parallel, one node merges. It’s the shape behind a market scan, a dependency audit, a code review, a research report - swap the sources and prompts and the same skeleton adapts.
The canonical form has a name worth memorizing: fan out → reduce → synthesize. Fan out to gather breadth, reduce with plain code to compress it, synthesize with a final agent to write the answer. 
Once you see the diamond, you stop asking “how do I make my agent do more steps” and start asking “where’s the split, where’s the merge” - which is the question that actually scales.

08. Route the edge at runtime with a conditional
Not every graph is fixed. Sometimes the edge to take depends on what a node found. A router node inspects a result and decides which downstream path fires - classify the ticket, then branch to the right handler; check the diff size, then either do a quick review or spin up a full audit. 
In a workflow this is just a JavaScript if or switch on a node’s validated output, because control flow lives in code.
This is where determinism becomes a feature, not a limitation. The router’s decision can be Claude-powered (a subagent classifies), but the routing is code Claude wrote - so it runs the same way every time for the same classification. 
You get Claude’s judgment at the node and the script’s reliability at the edge. No emergent “Claude decided to skip the audit” surprises  - because the skip would have to be written into the graph, and it isn’t.
python
// Router node: an agent classifies, code picks the edge.
const { severity } = await agent(
  `Classify this diff's risk:\n${diff}`,
  { schema: { type: 'object',
      properties: { severity: { enum: ['low', 'high'] } },
      required: ['severity'] } },
);

let review;
if (severity === 'high') {
  // heavy path: full parallel audit
  review = await parallel(FILES.map((f) => () => agent(`Audit ${f}`)));
} else {
  // light path: one quick pass
  review = await agent(`Quick review of ${diff}`);
}

09. Put a verifier on the edge
The real leverage of a graph isn’t more agents - it’s the structure you can wrap around them to produce confidence. 
A verifier node sits on the edge before a result is allowed downstream, and its only job is to try to kill the finding. If it survives, it passes. If not, it never reaches the answer.
Three patterns are worth having in your hands. 
Adversarial verify: for each finding, spawn N independent skeptics prompted to refute it; keep it only if a majority survive. 
Perspective-diverse verify: give each verifier a distinct lens - correctness, security, does-it-reproduce - because diversity catches failure modes that N identical checks never will. 
Judge panel: generate N attempts from different angles, score them with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best of the runners-up. 
This is exactly the pattern that let a real team port the Bun runtime with adversarial code review baked into the loop.

10. Isolate nodes so one failure can’t poison the graph
In a chain, a failure cascades - C dies, D never runs, the whole thing halts. In a graph, failure should be contained to its node. 
That’s already partly true: a thunk that throws inside parallel() resolves to null, so eight good agents still return while one bad one drops out. Your .filter(Boolean) is the containment. 

Design every fan-in to tolerate missing inputs rather than assume a full set.
The subtler failure is nodes stepping on each other. When agents write files in parallel, they can collide. 

The fix is isolation: "worktree" - each agent runs in its own git worktree, does its work in a sandbox, and merges cleanly. 

Reach for it only when nodes actually write in parallel. it’s the seatbelt for the one topology that needs it, not a default tax on every run.

11. Add a cycle - but make it converge
Sometimes you don’t know how big the job is until you’re in it: unknown-size discovery, a bug sweep where finding one bug reveals three more. That needs a cycle - a controlled edge back to an earlier node. 
The danger is obvious: a cycle that doesn’t converge is an infinite loop that spawns agents until your budget is gone.
The pattern that converges is loop-until-dry: keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds surface nothing new, then stop. The one detail that makes or breaks it - and the mistake almost everyone makes the first time - is what you dedupe against. 
Dedupe against everything seen, not just against confirmed results. Otherwise rejected findings reappear every round, the loop never runs dry, and you’ve built a machine that pays to rediscover the same dead ends forever.
const seen = new Set(); const confirmed = []; let dry = 0;

while (dry < 2) {                       // stop after 2 empty rounds
  const found = (await parallel(
    FINDERS.map((f) => () => agent(f.prompt, { schema: BUGS }))
  )).filter(Boolean).flatMap((r) => r.bugs);

  const fresh = found.filter((b) => !seen.has(key(b)));
  if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue; } // nothing new → toward dry
  dry = 0;
  fresh.forEach((b) => seen.add(key(b))); // dedupe vs SEEN, not confirmed

  // diverse-lens verify each fresh finding before it counts
  const judged = await parallel(fresh.map((b) => () =>
    parallel(['correctness', 'security', 'repro'].map((lens) => () =>
      agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via ${lens} — real?`, { schema: VERDICT })))
    .then((v) => ({ b, real: v.filter(Boolean).filter((x) => x.real).length >= 2 }))));

  confirmed.push(...judged.filter((v) => v.real).map((v) => v.b));
}

12. Tier the models across the nodes
Not every node needs your best model. A graph makes this obvious in a way a single agent never does: some nodes are bounded and repetitive (extract this field, classify this ticket), and some carry the real judgment (synthesize the report, adjudicate the finding). 
Run the boring nodes on a cheaper model and spend your expensive tokens where judgment actually lives.
In a workflow every subagent Claude spawns inherits your session model unless the script overrides it - so by default a big run bills entirely at your session tier. The model option on a single agent() call tells Claude to route just that node elsewhere. 
Check /model before a large run, then have Claude route the fan-out’s repetitive nodes down to a cheaper model and keep the merge node up. This is the lever that turns a token-hungry graph from expensive into economical without touching its shape.

13. Topology is your cost and latency
The shape of the graph isn’t cosmetic - it’s the single biggest lever on wall-clock time. The choice that trips everyone up: parallel() versus pipeline(). A parallel() barrier makes everything wait for the slowest node before the next stage starts.
A pipeline() streams each item through all stages independently, with no barrier - item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. Fast items finish early instead of idling behind slow ones.
Default to pipeline(). Reach for a barrier only when a stage truly needs every prior result at once - a cross-set dedupe, an early-exit on the total, a prompt that compares against “the other findings.” “It’s cleaner code” and “the stages feel separate” are not reasons; barrier latency is real, measurable, wasted time. Separate is not the same as synchronized.

14. Let Claude draw the graph - self-routing
The final move is to stop drawing the graph by hand for jobs you can’t plan in advance. 
With dynamic workflows, you describe the objective and Claude writes the orchestration script itself- decomposing the task, choosing the fan-out, spawning a coordinated fleet of subagents, and synthesizing the result. You get a graph tailored to this run instead of a fixed one you hoped would fit.
There are three ways in. Say the word “workflow” in your prompt and Claude writes one for the task. Run a saved or bundled one - /deep-research is a real graph shipping in production: scope → parallel search → fetch → adversarial verify → synthesize, the exact skeleton from this course. 
Or turn on ultracode and Claude plans a workflow for every substantial task in the session. When a run is good, press s to save its script into .claude/workflows/ - version-controlled, re-runnable by name, a graph anyone who clones the repo can launch.

Implement a major architectural upgrade to the Go project `entire-loop` (an Entire CLI plugin — a self-prompting agent-org "graph loop"). Work ONLY in the worktree **/Users/suhaan/Documents/Coding/entire-loop-graphorg** (branch `graph-org`). Read the existing code first — this is an evolution of a working MVP, keep its style, keep gates green, add tests.

CONTEXT: the MVP runs worker "seats" (research/build/critic/measure) as a FLAT PARALLEL fan-out, each spawning `claude --print` (non-mutating, plan mode), briefs built from `entire graph`/`entire brain query`, hybrid per-seat model+MCP tiers, process-group reaping, no-egress gate. A self-run exposed that this topology is wrong. Implement the following, coherently:

## Part A — 5 robustness fixes (precise specs below, from the plugin's own research seat)
1. `internal/agent/spawn.go` runWithReaping (unix): after SIGKILL escalation the final `<-done` is UNBOUNDED → a D-state child hangs the round forever. Add a bounded second grace timer after SIGKILL; on expiry return best-effort captured stdout/stderr with `timedOut=true` + a "process could not be reaped" warning, and let `cmd.Wait()` finish in a DETACHED goroutine (the `done` chan is buffered size-1, so abandoning the wait is leak-safe). CRITICAL: do NOT change runWithReaping's 4-value return signature (stdout,stderr,timedOut,err) — 3 tests + spawn_other.go destructure it positionally; thread the new warning via the existing return or an out-param that doesn't break callers. Mirror the bounded-grace fix in `spawn_other.go` (non-unix). Watch the `finish()`/`readWG.Wait()` interaction: if you bail before `werr` arrives, the child's dup'd fds may still be open so io.Copy on the read ends can still block — handle that (set read deadlines / close your pipe ends).
2. `internal/org/loop.go` fanOut goroutines have no panic recovery → one panic crashes the whole process and wg.Wait() never unblocks. Wrap each seat goroutine body (Briefer.Brief + Runner.Run) in `defer/recover` converting a panic into `SeatResult{Role, OK:false, Warnings:["seat panicked: <recovered>"]}`.
3. `internal/agent/runner.go` loadCached/saveCached persist a failed/timed-out SeatResult as the completion marker → a transient failure poisons the seat for the whole run. Only cache OK results (or retry once before caching a failure). loadCached must ignore non-OK cache.
4. `internal/agent/runner.go` cappedBuffer.exceeded is set but never read → truncated stdout is silently fed to the parser. Surface truncation as a SeatResult warning.
5. no-egress refusal currently exits 0 → make it exit non-zero so scripts detect the refusal.

## Part B — round-scoped cache + PIPELINE EDGES (the core topology fix)
- Round-scope the seat cache: include the round number in the cache path/key so round N does not replay round N-1 (the bug: round 2 had identical cost to round 1).
- Replace the flat parallel fan-out with a DAG that carries DATA ACROSS EDGES within a round: `research → build → critic → measure/synthesize`. Concretely: build's brief MUST include research's findings; critic's brief MUST include build's proposal (+ research). Sequence seats that have edges; keep parallelism only where seats are genuinely independent. Preserve the `--jobs`/CONC cap for any fan-out stage. This is the course's node/edge/diamond model — a downstream node consumes its upstream node's validated output, not a shared window.

## Part C — mutating build seat in an isolated worktree (lets it write real code)
- The `build` seat becomes MUTATING: it runs `claude --print` in **bypassPermissions** mode (NOT plan mode) inside a FRESH throwaway `git worktree` of the TARGET repo, so it actually writes code. After it finishes, capture `git diff` (and new files) of that worktree as the seat's `proposal`, then `git worktree remove --force` it. NEVER write to the target repo's main working tree. If the target isn't a git repo or worktree creation fails, degrade to the old non-mutating propose-as-text path with a warning. Isolate per course step 10 (parallel mutating seats each get their own worktree; unique dir per seat+round). Keep research/critic/measure NON-mutating (plan mode).

## Part D — loop-until-dry cycle
- Replace fixed `--rounds N` as the sole terminator with a converge loop: keep running rounds until (a) goal-met (critic/synthesize verdict), OR (b) K consecutive rounds with NO NEW progress, OR (c) a `--max-rounds` safety cap (default e.g. 6). Track a `seen` set of finding/proposal keys; a round is "dry" if it surfaces nothing NOT already in `seen`. DEDUPE AGAINST `seen` (everything ever seen), NOT against confirmed/accepted — else rejected items reappear every round and it never converges (course step 11). Keep `--rounds` as an alias for max-rounds or a fixed-count mode.

## Part E — router + verifier-on-edge
- Router (course step 8): a control/router step inspects a signal (e.g. build proposal diff size, or goal complexity from a classifier seat) and routes: small change → one quick critic pass; large → full parallel verifier audit. Routing is code (if/switch on validated output), deterministic.
- Verifier-on-edge (course step 9): before a finding/proposal is ACCEPTED into the result, spawn N=3 independent skeptic verifiers with DIVERSE lenses (correctness / security / does-it-reproduce), each prompted to REFUTE; keep it only if a majority (≥2) survive. Put this on the edge before results are committed to state.

Keep: hybrid model tiers (cheap=claude-haiku-4-5, deep=sonnet), the no-egress gate, schema'd/lenient-JSON seat contracts, ENTIRE_* env + doctor. Update the reorg.go stub or fold reorg rules into the loop as real logic where they fit (small→solo etc.).

TESTS (mock the runner via the existing `Runner` interface / FakeRunner — NEVER spawn real claude in tests): round-scoped cache (round 2 ≠ round 1 replay), pipeline data-flow (build brief contains research output; critic brief contains build proposal), loop-until-dry (dedupe vs seen; converges; rejected item doesn't resurface; max-rounds cap), router (small vs large → different path), verifier majority (2/3 survive → accept, 2/3 refute → drop), mutating-build worktree logic (use a temp git repo + a fake runner that "writes" a file, assert diff captured + worktree removed), and keep all Part-A regression tests. **Toolchain result:** `go build ./...` ✅ · `go vet ./...` ✅ (clean) · `go test ./...` ✅ 101 passed · `go test -race ./...` ✅ 101 passed. ## 1. SAFETY — the mutating build seat (danger zone first)

### CONFIRMED

**[crit] internal/agent/worktree.go:33-72 + seats.go:146-189 — the "throwaway worktree" is NOT a sandbox; bypassPermissions + shared `.git` + inherited env give the build worker full-power reach.**
A `git worktree` shares the object store, refs, config and hooks with the parent. `--permission-mode bypassPermissions` (seats.go:47,147) lets the worker run arbitrary shell as the user. Concretely reproduced in a scratch repo:
- **Shared refs are mutable from the worktree.** `git tag -f injected-tag HEAD` and `git branch -f feature-x HEAD` both *succeeded from inside the detached worktree and the parent repo saw the mutation* (`feature-x before=0c8b… after=8c9f…`). Git only protects the branch that is currently checked out (`main` → "cannot force update the branch used by worktree"); **every other ref — all tags, all non-checked-out branches, notes, and anything reachable via `git update-ref` / `git push` / `git gc --prune` / `git reflog expire` — is fair game and hits the parent's shared `.git`.**
- **Arbitrary shell escapes the worktree entirely.** cwd is the worktree, but nothing constrains `rm -rf <repoRoot>`, editing the parent's main tree by absolute path, `git -C <repoRoot> …`, or reading `~/.ssh` / `~/.aws`.
- **Full parent env is inherited.** For the build seat `McpBrain=false`, so `buildCmd` (seats.go:186-188) never sets `cmd.Env` → Go hands the child the orchestrator's *entire* environment, including any `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`/cloud creds. Combined with network access, that is an exfiltration path.
- **Trigger is realistic:** the build brief embeds `${UPSTREAM}` = the research seat's findings and repo file content (brief.go:117-135, build.md:16). A prompt-injected instruction hidden in the target repo's files or in a research finding flows straight into the bypass worker and is executed.

Fix direction: don't rely on the worktree for isolation. Run the mutating worker in a real sandbox (container / new mount+PID+net namespace / seccomp), pass a **scrubbed allowlisted env** (never `os.Environ()` for the bypass seat), and consider a throwaway **clone** (separate object store) rather than a `worktree` so ref/object mutations can't reach the user's repo. At minimum, gate egress for the bypass seat and strip secrets.

**[high] internal/agent/worktree.go:77-86 — `git diff --cached` silently loses the change if the worker COMMITS in the worktree.**
`gitCaptureDiff` does `git add -A` then `git diff --cached`. If the build agent commits its work (entirely natural — build.md:26-31 says "actually write the files" and never says *don't commit*), the index is clean and the diff is **empty**. Reproduced exactly:
```
worker: echo package x > feature.go; git add -A; git commit -m impl
capture: git add -A && git diff --cached  →  length 0   (change LOST)
```
Result: `runMutatingBuild` warns "produced no file changes; proposal is empty" (worktree.go:53-54), the real work is discarded, the round reads as no-progress, and the router sees a 0-line diff. The passing test `TestRunMutatingBuild_CapturesDiffAndCleansUp` only writes a file and never commits, so it can't catch this.
Fix: resolve the base commit at add time and capture against it: `git add -A && git diff <baseSha>` — verified in the same scratch repo (`git diff $BASE` → 136 bytes vs `--cached` → 0). And/or tell the worker in build.md not to commit.

**[med] internal/agent/worktree.go:45,91-97 + runner.go:146-153 — orphaned worktree + admin entry leak on a hard kill of the orchestrator.**
Teardown is a `defer` (worktree.go:45). It runs on normal return and on panic, but **not** on SIGKILL/OOM/`os.Exit` of the parent. Each killed run leaves `<RunDir>/worktrees/r<N>-<role>-<nano>/` plus a `.git/worktrees/<leaf>` admin entry (and possibly an `index.lock`). Nothing prunes at startup, so entries accumulate across killed runs. Fix: `git worktree prune` on run startup, and/or register worktrees in a manifest reconciled at launch.

### POSSIBLE / lower

- **[low] runner.go:146-153 — worktree path is safe by default but not if `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR` points inside the repo.** Default DataDir is `~/.local/share/entire/plugins/data/loop` (env.go:37-48) → worktrees live *outside* the target tree (good). If an operator sets `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR` under the repo, worktrees nest inside the working tree and the parent's own tooling can see/stage them. Consider forcing worktrees to an OS-temp root regardless of DataDir.
- **[low] worktree.go:49 — a cancelled round loses an already-built proposal.** `gitCaptureDiff` uses the cancellable `ctx`; on round cancellation `git add`/`diff` fail and the built diff is dropped. Teardown correctly uses `context.WithoutCancel`; capture could too.
- **Concurrency collision: not currently reachable.** Only one mutating (build) seat exists per round (dedupeByRole) and rounds run sequentially, so no two worktree adds race; the `r%d-<role>-<nano>` leaf is unique anyway. Fine for today's planner; would need re-checking if a second mutating role is ever added.
